scenes.text: Beneath Europa's icy shell lies an ocean with more than twice the water of all Earth's oceans combined. NASA's Europa Clipper will fly past it 49 times to measure whether that ocean could support life.

scenes.text: We have never sampled liquid water beyond Earth. Finding it — or ruling it out — changes how we think about life everywhere.

scenes.text: Juno's 2022 flyby measured Europa's ice shell at about 29 kilometers thick, plus or minus 10. That estimate comes from a pure water-ice model — salt could reduce it by about 5 kilometers, and the full shell may be thicker still.
scenes.why_this_image: Scientific evidence — diagram supports the specific claim being made

scenes.text: On Enceladus, Cassini found sodium phosphates in ice grains. The authors estimate the ocean phosphorus is at least about 100 times Earth's ocean concentration — a geochemical inference, not a direct sample of liquid water.
scenes.why_this_image: Scientific evidence — diagram supports the specific claim being made

scenes.text: Europa Clipper launched October 14, 2024. A Mars gravity assist in 2025, then an Earth gravity assist in 2026, sends it to Jupiter orbit in April 2030 — first Europa flyby in 2031.

scenes.text: What we know: Europa has an ocean, Enceladus has phosphates and organics. What we presume: those ingredients could support life. What we have not proven: that life exists there at all.
scenes.why_this_image: Conclusion — text card summarizes known/presumed/unproven
